entry.evidence: it is unknown if concentrated föhn jets spilled onto the former LAIS and LBIS and, if so, whether those föhn winds contributed to their collapse

sequences.source_document: published paper (XML text, with PDF for figures)

steps.action: The authors adopt the Massom et al. (2018) conceptual model of four prerequisites for rapid collapse (surface flooding and hydrofracture, sea-ice loss, frontal rifting, calving trigger) as the framing hypothesis.
steps.quote: a conceptual model for rapid ice shelf collapse proposed by Massom et al. (2018) identifies four essential prerequisites for sudden collapse

steps.action: They take from earlier field and satellite studies the observation that clear skies and warm west-northwest föhn winds were present at the time of both collapses.
steps.quote: meteorological and satellite observations identify clear skies and warm west-northwest föhn wind at the time of collapse

steps.action: They pose three questions: how much föhn melt contributed to each eastern AP ice shelf's melt budget, whether föhn and its melt helped trigger the LAIS and LBIS collapses, and what this implies for the extant shelves.
steps.quote: Did föhn winds and associated melt play a role in triggering the collapses of the LAIS and LBIS?

steps.action: They use 3-hourly, 5.5 km RACMO2.3p2 hindcast output for 1979-2018, curated by a co-author's group, as the melt and meteorology record; its validation against LCIS AWS data is cited, not performed here.
steps.quote: We base our analysis on 3-hourly output from simulations by the Regional Atmospheric Climate Model 2 (RACMO2), version 2.3p2

steps.action: They apply the FöhnDA algorithm from their own earlier paper (12 AWS, T > 0 °C plus quantile-regression thresholds on wind speed and humidity) and an ML classifier trained on co-located AWS to flag föhn-induced melt in RACMO2 output.
steps.quote: previously developed and detailed in Laffin et al. (2021)

steps.action: They design the comparison: shelves split into five areas, annual climatologies of melt, melt hours and temperature, two-tailed t-tests against LBIS, and a liquid-to-solid ratio as a proxy for firn air content.
steps.quote: We use a two-tailed t -test statistic to identify if the mean surface temperature and mean surface melt of both ice shelves are statistically different

steps.action: They extract ERA5 3-hourly sea-ice concentration over 90 km boxes east of Larsen A, B and C and relate summer föhn occurrence to summer sea ice by Pearson correlation.
steps.quote: We measure the mean sea ice concentration of the ocean 90 km directly east of each ice shelf

steps.action: From föhn-period wind fields and melt patterns they identify seven recurring föhn jets, three of them (LA, LB, JP) new, and show that west and northwest winds raise melt rates by up to 53 %.
steps.quote: we identify seven recurring föhn jets or “gap winds” that lead to high surface melt rates on the eastern AP ice shelves

steps.action: They check that the model reproduces the four LCIS jets already documented by airborne observations and earlier model studies, as a reference for trusting the newly identified jets.
steps.quote: [...] of these jets (CI, MI, WI, MOI) have been studied using airborne observations and model simulations

steps.action: They estimate the föhn-induced share of melt for 1979-2002: 42 % on LAIS and 51 % on LBIS (up to 61 % and 57 % under the jets), against 25 % on SCAR inlet and 17 % on LCIS.
steps.quote: Föhn-induced surface melt accounts for 42 % of the total annual melt between 1979 and 2002 on the LAIS

steps.action: They compare collapsed with intact shelves and take the contrast in föhn melt as implicating föhn melt in the collapses.
steps.quote: The stark contrast in surface melt amount and fraction caused by föhn winds on collapsed vs. intact ice shelves implicates föhn melt

steps.action: They take from earlier studies the expectation that melt and melt lakes near the terminus can cause calving-front collapse and wider instability.
steps.quote: Surface melt and melt lakes near the ice shelf terminus can lead to calving front collapse and structural instability

steps.action: They show that the LA and LB jets reach the calving fronts, whereas SCAR inlet lacks a strong jet and the LCIS jets weaken before reaching its distant front (Fig. 3b).
steps.quote: the LA and LB föhn jets impact a large spatial area of the LAIS and LBIS and reach the ice shelf calving fronts

steps.action: They locate three föhn events on 18-27 January 1995 in the hindcast, overlapping the collapse onset on 25 January as dated by Rott et al. (1998).
steps.quote: Three föhn wind events occurred on LAIS between 18 and 27 January 1995, overlapping with the initial phase of the LAIS collapse

steps.action: They estimate that the 9-day föhn period gave 268.5 mm w.e., 25.2 % of the 1994/1995 melt and more than any other 9-day period in 1979-2018, in a season 127 % above average.
steps.quote: produced increased surface melt greater than any other 9 d period from 1979–2018

steps.action: They find a negative correlation between summer föhn hours and sea-ice concentration on all three shelves (r about -0.7), stronger than the correlation with air temperature.
steps.quote: We also identify a negative correlation between the occurrence of föhn winds and sea ice concentration on all eastern AP ice shelves

steps.action: They read ERA5 sea ice east of LAIS across the 9-day event: near 100 % at the start, then a marked drop by collapse onset (Fig. 5c-e).
steps.quote: At the start of the 9 d föhn event, sea ice concentration east of the LAIS was at or near 100 %

steps.action: They estimate lake extent (5.1-10.8 % of LAIS area) from an analogue AVHRR image of 8 December 1992, combine it with modelled liquid water from the 9-day event, and obtain mean lake depths of 1.38-6.86 m.
steps.quote: We find mean melt lake depth to be between 1.38–6.86 m depending on lake location and föhn influence

steps.action: They compare the estimated depths with the observed 1 m LBIS lake depth (Banwell et al., 2014) and the modelled 5 m depth for hydrofracture cascades (Banwell et al., 2013).
steps.quote: [...] average lake depth of the LBIS lakes prior to collapse (1 m)

steps.action: They locate a föhn event coinciding with the initial LBIS collapse on 9 February 2002, two events just before it and three more before full collapse, with melt rates 27 % above non-föhn melt that season.
steps.quote: A föhn wind event coincided with the initial LBIS collapse on 9 February 2002

steps.action: Using t-tests against LBIS, they show that total melt differs between shelves, but once föhn melt is removed, SCAR inlet and Larsen C (north) are statistically indistinguishable from LBIS.
steps.quote: when föhn-induced melt is subtracted from total melt, the mean annual surface melt production on SCAR inlet and Larsen C (north) is not statistically different

steps.action: They vary the reference shelf of the intercomparison from LBIS to LAIS and report qualitatively similar results.
steps.quote: Qualitatively similar results are obtained when comparing all ice shelves to the LAIS.

steps.action: They compute the liquid-to-solid ratio: just above 1 on all shelves without föhn melt, but above 1.5 over large parts of LAIS and LBIS, including the margins, when föhn melt is included.
steps.quote: When surface melt caused by föhn wind is included, LSR exceeds 1.5 throughout extensive regions, including the ice shelf margins, of the LAIS and LBIS

steps.action: They add the sub-claim that föhn melt preconditioned LAIS and LBIS for lake formation through long-term firn densification.
steps.quote: föhn-induced melt helped precondition the LAIS and LBIS to produce extensive melt lakes by long-term firn densification

steps.action: They argue that the north-south temperature gradient alone cannot explain the excess melt on LAIS and LBIS, and that suture zones cannot be the sole cause because all shelves have them but only two collapsed.
steps.quote: the temperature gradient alone does not explain the substantial increase in surface melt on the LAIS and LBIS relative to more southerly ice shelves

steps.action: To explain why the strong 1992/1993 season caused no collapse, they invoke auxiliaries: early-season melt buffered by pore space (§4 ¶2), and sea ice and mélange still at the front in the 8 December 1992 AVHRR image, so the Massom prerequisites were misaligned (§4 ¶3).
steps.quote: sea ice and melange are shown to be at the calving front, protecting the front from long-period ocean swells

steps.action: They qualify the lake-depth estimate: likely an underestimate because only the 9-day melt is counted, with the LBIS critical depth possibly an upper limit for LAIS.
steps.quote: Melt lake depth is likely underestimated because our estimation only accounts for melt during the 9 d melt event.

steps.action: They keep the claim that föhn winds and their melt played a significant, contributory role in both collapses, and that the extant shelves are unlikely to collapse from föhn melt within historical bounds.
steps.quote: We conclude that föhn winds and the associated surface melt played a significant role in the collapses of the LAIS and LBIS

sequences.source_document: open review record tc-2021-301 (RC1, AC1, CC1, AC3, RC2, AC2)

steps.action: Referee 1 objects that the preprint's claim of no prior studies is wrong and that key föhn literature is missing; the authors rewrite the Introduction to place the questions within existing föhn and melt studies.
steps.quote: This statement about the Larsen A and B ice shelves is entirely incorrect as there have been many studies

steps.action: Prompted by Referee 1's suggestion of an indirect föhn role in the LBIS collapse, the authors adopt the Massom et al. (2018) framework and add the mechanism of föhn pushing sea ice away so that ocean swell can reach the front.
steps.quote: This is a very interesting question that inspired us to change the manuscript.

steps.action: The authors downgrade the headline claim from föhn melt triggering the collapses to föhn playing a supporting role, and change the title accordingly.
steps.quote: We will also change the title of the manuscript to not suggest fohn winds triggered collapse

steps.action: Asked to support the 'most accurate' detection claim, the authors state that FöhnDA comes from Laffin et al. (2021) and add that paper's intercomparison statistics to the supplement (Fig. S1, Table S1), without new analysis.
steps.quote: We did complete an intercomparison sensitivity study detailed in Laffin et al., 2021, comparing other identification methods.

steps.action: Commenter Rott cites ERS-1 SAR images showing about 1 % lake cover on 25 January 1995 and argues against a hydrofracture trigger; the authors answer with a 28 January SAR image showing ponds, and the final paper says lake extent during collapse cannot be estimated (Fig. S3).
steps.quote: high resolution synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images (ca. 25 m resolution) of the ESA ERS-1 satellite were acquired during the disintegration event

steps.action: Against Rott's challenge to the uniqueness of the LA and LB jet positions, the authors defend them by arguing that jets are defined by melt, not wind speed, and by pointing to correct LCIS jets, with no new analysis.
steps.quote: The location of the fohn jets are indicated by fohn-induced surface melt and not wind speed.

steps.action: Asked by Referee 2 about the storm that Scambos et al. (2000) name as the LAIS trigger, the authors report in the rebuttal that the storm was the föhn events; this is not stated in the final paper.
steps.quote: the powerful fohn wind events discussed in this study as there were no other major storm systems in the region

steps.action: Referee 2 notes that the 1987 and 1989 retreats occurred in years without major föhn melt; the authors reply that these events cannot be dated or attributed and do no new work.
steps.quote: it is difficult to attribute a cause for these events

steps.action: Referee 2 judges Question 2 too strong; the authors rephrase it to ask what role föhn played.
steps.quote: we plan to alter Question 2 to fit more in line with the new direction of the manuscript

steps.action: Referee 2 asks for föhn frequency statistics to put the melt fractions in context; the final paper adds föhn-hour and melt-hour percentages (Fig. 2b, §3.1 ¶2).
steps.quote: Yes, we agree and will add in melt frequency stats.

steps.action: Referee 2 questions using 1992/1993 as an analogue and then citing melt timing; the authors add the argument that sea ice was present at the front in 1992/1993 but absent in 1995 (final §4 ¶3).
steps.quote: we will also discuss a lack of sea ice in 1995 that triggered collapse, while in 92/93 sea ice was present

steps.action: Referee 2 asks for melt per area; the authors reply that the values were already area means and only clarify the wording.
steps.quote: We already calculated for the mean melt over the entire ice shelf

steps.action: Referee 2 notes that the 0 °C detection threshold and future warming undermine the claim that extant shelves are safe; the authors make the stability statement conditional on historical bounds and add the SAM and warming caveats (final §5 ¶2).
steps.quote: You are correct that our algorithm only identifies fohn winds above freezing

steps.action: Referee 2 points to other differences between the shelves (sea ice, ocean forcing, structure, basal melt); the final paper discusses suture zones and marine ice and notes contributors not considered (§4 ¶1, §4 ¶4).
steps.quote: There are likely many other differences between the Larsen A and B and the other ice shelves beyond foehn wind patterns.

tree.answer: Rapid Larsen A (1995) and B (2002) collapses with föhn present; role of föhn melt unknown
No; föhn melt inferred from RACMO2 hindcast flagged by an AWS-trained ML detector
Quantify föhn melt contribution and its timing relative to collapse; implications for extant shelves
Temperature/latitude gradient, suture zones, sea-ice and swell (integrated, not rival), basal melt (not considered)
Partly: without föhn melt, collapsed and intact shelves should not differ if föhn is the differentiator
Found, not set: past collapses reconstructed from hindcast, reanalysis and imagery

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Two collapse events and five shelf areas over 1979-2018 serve as repetitions
Only lightly varied: reference shelf swapped; detector checks cited from earlier work
Kept: föhn melt and wind direction played a significant contributory role
Survived after revision: trigger claim downgraded to supporting role under referee and commenter pressure

end.claim: Föhn winds and their associated surface melt, together with the off-coast wind that cleared sea ice from the fronts, played a significant contributory role in the Larsen A and B collapses, while the extant shelves are less exposed to föhn melt.

decisive_move.sentence: Separating föhn-induced melt from total melt in the RACMO2 hindcast with the AWS-trained föhn detector is what makes the contrast between collapsed and intact shelves, and the timing of melt around collapse, possible at all.

gates.evidence: All data are pre-existing model hindcast (RACMO2), reanalysis (ERA5) and archived imagery; no data were acquired to test a hypothesis. The non-föhn-melt t-test (§3.3 ¶1) could have shown that collapsed shelves still differed, and the coincidence analysis could have found no föhn at collapse, so the claim faced partial tests. No hypothesis or threshold was fixed in advance; the claim itself was reshaped after review.

imports.item: Binary-classification machine-learning detector (scikit-learn) trained on AWS föhn labels and applied to model output
Quantile regression for site-specific wind-speed and humidity thresholds
Two-tailed t-test for differences between ice shelves
Pearson correlation between föhn occurrence and sea-ice concentration

novelty_claims.quote: The remaining three jets (LA, LB, and JP) are, to our knowledge, identified here for the first time.
allows for new föhn jet identification on the LAIS and LBIS despite lack of direct observation
this research highlights a new understanding behind föhn melt mechanisms for ice shelf collapse

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: the three new föhn jets (LA, LB, JP) and the 25 % (±3 % in the abstract, source of the uncertainty not given) 9-day melt share are estimate_with_resolution, but resolution is limited to 5.5 km and the jets are not validated by direct observation; the föhn and sea-ice correlation (r about -0.7, 1979-2018) is regularity_in_range; firn-densification preconditioning rests on a crude LSR proxy (best_explanation); the statement that the extant shelves will stay stable is a conditional projection with no skill test. The föhn detector's validation (sensitivity study, and probably the 23 % accuracy gain over simple binary classification) is cited from Laffin et al. (2021); whether the 23 % comparison was redone here is unclear (inference). RACMO2 warm bias and cloud underestimation are acknowledged, but their effect on föhn-melt fractions is not tested. Lake extent rests on a single 1992 analogue image. In the review record, the authors report work not in the final paper: identifying the Scambos et al. (2000) storm as the föhn events, and a 28 January 1995 SAR image with ponds. Rott's point about the gradual 20-year retreat of Larsen A is answered with a promise, yet §5 ¶1 still contrasts the collapses with long-term thinning and retreat. Referee 2's question about the 1987/1989 retreats is not resolved. The reframing from trigger to supporting role was driven by review, so the published claim is weaker than the preprint's. Supplement content (Figs. S1-S3, Tables S1-S2) was not available to the coder.

disagreements.support: The authors accept the swell trigger but add that föhn winds supplied the melt lakes and cleared the sea ice, supported by ERA5 sea-ice decline during the January 1995 föhn event and the föhn and sea-ice correlation.
disagreements.quote: the west-northwest wind direction actively pushed or melted sea ice and fast ice away from the calving front

disagreements.target: Studies proposing suture zones as a major contributor to instability (Glasser and Scambos, 2008; Borstad et al., 2016)
disagreements.support: All shelves in the region have sutured tributary glaciers, yet only two collapsed.
disagreements.quote: while some studies suggest this is a major contributor to ice shelf instability, only two of the ice shelves have collapsed

disagreements.target: Warming and the latitudinal temperature gradient as the explanation for northern shelf vulnerability (Scambos et al., 2003; Morris and [...] )
disagreements.support: Once föhn melt is removed, melt on the intact shelves is statistically indistinguishable from LBIS (t-tests, Fig. 6b).
disagreements.quote: the temperature gradient alone does not explain the substantial increase in surface melt on the LAIS and LBIS relative to more southerly ice shelves
